description: RedGrid, a collaborative team passionate about technology, data, and creative problem-solving. For NASA’s Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map challenge, we are developing an interactive tool to help future Mars explorers plan safer and more scientifically valuable journeys across the Martian surface.
summary:
RedGrid responds to the "Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map" challenge by uniting 10+ fragmented NASA and USGS Mars datasets into a single layered mission-planning map and first-person 3D Mars surface walk for Jezero Crater (18.44°N, 77.45°E). Today, planning a human walk (EVA) on Mars forces planners to cross-check five separate tools by hand—topographic DTMs, hazard maps, mineral science targets, MEDA weather, and spacesuit oxygen/battery spreadsheets—where one wrong turn past the oxygen walkback limit is fatal.

RedGrid solves this on a co-registered 8.0-meter Mars 2000 grid (4,744,570 routable cells). When an explorer selects a start and destination, RedGrid simultaneously computes four routes—Safest, Shortest, Science-Focused, and Mission Priority—under one strict Apollo-style oxygen and battery walkback reserve lock. Because zero humans have walked on Mars, RedGrid bridges Apollo 11–17 lunar human step choices and PLSS metabolic rates with Perseverance and Curiosity Martian terrain experience. Explorers can compare all four routes side by side on a 2D map and radar chart, descend to Jezero Crater in an interactive Three.js 3D surface walk that streams live 3D footsteps back to the 2D planner, and export a complete printable EVA mission report with full NASA dataset provenance.
details:
What RedGrid Does

RedGrid is a full-stack Martian EVA decision-support system for Jezero Crater that answers three questions before any astronaut takes a step:

1. Is it safe? (Avoids >20° slopes and boulder/ripple hazard cores, and guarantees round-trip oxygen and battery return to a refill habitat with a 20% safety reserve.)

2. Is it worth it? (Scores proximity to high-priority CRISM mineral detections and Perseverance sample-caching targets.)

3. Does it fit the mission? (Computes four distinct routes at once—Safest, Shortest, Science-Focused, and Mission Priority—allowing planners to blend preset profiles or tune 7 priority sliders.)

Our Three Core Hypotheses

1. Scientific Hypothesis (Bridging Moon Humans + Mars Rovers):

Zero humans have ever walked on Mars; only Apollo 11–17 astronauts have walked on the Moon, and only wheeled rovers (Perseverance, Curiosity) have traversed Mars. We hypothesize that crewed Martian EVA route selection can be factored into:

- Human physiological step-selection and metabolic oxygen consumption transferred from Apollo 11–17 lunar walks and Apollo PLSS / NASA BVAD telemetry (0.077 kg O2/h at 300 W nominal work rate, spanning 0.07–0.09 kg O2/h across 265–310 W), and

- Martian surface traversability (aeolian sand ripples, crater rim scarps, thermal inertia, and bedrock roughness) derived from Perseverance and Curiosity traverses—without routing a human astronaut like a wheeled vehicle.

2. Mathematical Hypothesis (Step-Selection Conditional Logit + Weighted Product Routing):

- Step-Selection Conditional Logistic Regression Architecture (CostProvider): At every 10 m step of a real traverse, we compare the 1 chosen step against 15 feasible alternative steps on the surrounding ring (5,495 choice strata / 43,855 candidate steps across 18 terrain/hazard/science bitmasks prepared in `training_data/step_choices.csv`):

  P(y_{s,j} = 1 | X_s) = exp(beta^T x_{s,j}) / sum_{k=1}^{16} exp(beta^T x_{s,k}),   with category weight w_c = exp(-beta_c).

  Values w_c > 1 penalize avoided terrain; values w_c < 1 reward preferred terrain. (In the current Version 0 submission, the active routing engine uses our deterministic published-physics & hand-set baseline (`cost_models.version = 0, method = 'HAND_SET'`), with the pluggable `HttpModelCostProvider` and 5,495-stratum dataset ready for Version 1 MLE weight fitting.)

- Dimension-Free Weighted Product Model (PriorityResolver — Triantaphyllou 2000): Combines 6 category groups (Hazard, Terrain, Science, Comms, Uncertainty, Rover Path) with 7 normalized user sliders w_g:

  cost(i) = t_base(theta_i) * prod_g [ Factor_g(i) ]^(s_g),   where s_g = 7 * w_g.

- Hard Safety & Walkback Barriers: Any square with slope > 20°, inside a hazard core, or violating the oxygen/battery walkback inequality Used(start -> i) + Return(i -> nearest_refill) <= (1 - reserve) * Capacity is assigned infinite cost (blocked) and can never be overridden by any weight or science reward.

- Windowed 8-Neighbor Dijkstra + Catmull-Rom Spline Smoothing: Finds the exact global minimum-cost path across the 8.0 m grid and smooths grid staircase artifacts only when the smoothed segment remains 100% inside safe, routable cells.

3. Programmatic Hypothesis ("Puzzle-Piece" Provider Architecture):

Every data repository and AI/ML model slot is defined as a formal runtime-checked Python Protocol (CostProviderI, PriorityResolverI, ResourceProviderI) verified at startup by redgrid.registry.verify(). This allows RedGrid to hot-swap deterministic local algorithms (AlgorithmCostProvider, AlgorithmPriorityResolver) for remote HTTP machine-learning microservices (HttpModelCostProvider, HttpModelPriorityResolver) or live spacesuit telemetry streams with zero frontend changes and automatic safe fallback.

Tools, Languages & Software Used

- Frontend: React 19, TypeScript, TanStack Start / Router / Query, Tailwind CSS v4, Leaflet (2D mission map), Recharts (multi-metric route radar), Three.js (first-person 3D Mars orbital descent and surface walk).

- Backend: Python 3, Flask, SQLite 3 (with spatial grid indexing; PostGIS-ready schema), NumPy, SciPy (sparse graph Dijkstra), Rasterio, GeoPandas, Shapely, Pillow.

- Testing: 120 backend pytest tests + 48 frontend Vitest unit and live API contract tests.
